rulings.restated: Input — Did you pay over half the cost of keeping up your home for 2025? Cost of keeping up a home includes expenses such as rent, mortgage interest, real estate taxes, insurance on the home, repairs, utilities, and food eaten in the home. It does not include the cost of clothing, education, medical treatment, vacations, life insurance, or transportation, or the value of your services or those of a member of your household. Amounts paid out of funds received in the name of a person who lives in the home, such as their Social Security, count as paid by that person, not you. TANF or similar payments you received and used for the home count as paid by you.
rulings.model: The IRS note says TANF used 'to support another person' is considered support you provided for that person, and amounts in a child's or qualifying person's name are considered paid by the child; the restatement instead treats TANF used for the home as paid by you and refers to any person living in the home.
rulings.ruling: Ruling: model error; p501 p. 9, Keeping Up a Home, Note: "if you received Temporary Assistance to Needy Families (TANF) payments or other similar payments and used the payment to support another person, those payments are considered support you provided ... Amounts paid out of funds received in the child's or qualifying person's name, such as Social Security, are considered paid by the child, not you. If the total amount you paid is more than the amount others paid, you meet the requirement". The note sits in the cost-of-keeping-up-a-home test, so TANF used for the home counts as paid by you, as the question says (BUG-0258); funds in any other household member's name are paid by that member, not by you, so "a person who lives in the home" changes no answer to "over half". Project stands.

rulings.restated: Input — Do all five of these tests apply to you? 1. Your spouse died in 2023 or 2024 and you didn't remarry before the end of 2025 (if your spouse died in 2025, answer No). 2. You have a child or stepchild (not a foster child) whom you can claim as a dependent, or could claim as a dependent except that, for 2025, the child had gross income of $5,200 or more, the child filed a joint return, or you could be claimed as a dependent on someone else's return; an adopted child, including a child lawfully placed with you for legal adoption, is always your own child. 3. This child lived in your home for all of 2025, counting temporary absences by you or the child for special circumstances, such as school, vacation, business, medical care, military service or detention in a juvenile facility, as time lived in the home, but only an absence from which it was reasonable to assume the absent person would return and during which you kept up the home; a child born or who died in 2025, or adopted or lawfully placed with you for legal adoption in 2025, lived with you all year if your home was the child's home for the entire time the child was alive, or since the adoption or placement. 4. You paid over half the cost of keeping up your home (rent, mortgage interest, real estate taxes, insurance on the home, repairs, utilities and food eaten in the home; not clothing, education, medical treatment, vacations, life insurance, transportation or anyone’s services; amounts paid from a household member’s own funds, such as Social Security, count as paid by them). 5. You could have filed a joint return with your spouse the year your spouse died, even if you didn't actually do so.
rulings.model: Test 3 omits the IRS exception that a kidnapped child may still qualify the filer for QSS; the IRS text says you may be eligible even if the qualifying child has been kidnapped.
rulings.ruling: Ruling: finding; p501 p. 11, Qualifying Surviving Spouse, Kidnapped child: "You may be eligible to file as a qualifying surviving spouse even if the child who qualifies you for this filing status has been kidnapped." This is fix round 2's household F1 (.transcription/proposed/fixr2/household.findings.md), a low over-refusal batched by the owner in TASKS.md T-092. It is not re-raised as new. T-091 added only the expected-return clause to test 3 (p501 pp. 9, 11), which the T-091 round found no wider and no narrower than the source. The kidnapped-child gap predates T-091 and is unaffected by the correction. Project stands pending T-092.
